results.result: Glucose-induced vasoconstriction, LTCC activity, and Ser1928 phosphorylation require extracellular nucleotides. Apyrase treatment (which degrades extracellular nucleotides) prevented glucose-induced arterial constriction, LTCC current enhancement, and Ser1928 phosphorylation. These effects were specific to glucose and not due to osmotic changes (mannitol control). Under continuous perfusion (which washes away nucleotides), glucose failed to enhance LTCC activity, but under static conditions, the effect was restored.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C40 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (arterial diameter measurements, electrophysiology, Western blots, osmotic controls) demonstrating that extracellular nucleotides mediate glucose effects. The apyrase experiments are well-controlled with appropriate negative controls (K+ response, mannitol), and the flow vs. static bath experiments (C39-C40) provide mechanistic insight consistent with an autocrine nucleotide signaling mechanism.

results.result: P2Y11 receptor is expressed in human and mouse arterial myocytes at the plasma membrane. Western blot analysis detected P2Y11 at the expected molecular weight (~40 kDa) in human and mouse arterial lysates. Antisense ODN knockdown reduced P2Y11 protein by ~50%. Confocal imaging showed P2Y11 distribution at the plasma membrane co-localizing with wheat germ agglutinin (WGA). A higher molecular weight band (~110-120 kDa) in mouse tissue may represent receptor dimers.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C46 demonstrate P2Y11 expression using multiple complementary techniques (Western blot, antisense knockdown, confocal imaging with membrane marker). The antisense ODN knockdown (C42) provides specificity validation for the antibody. Appropriate negative controls (no primary antibody, boiled antibody) were included. The interpretation of the higher MW band as dimers (C45) is speculative but appropriately qualified and supported by citations.

results.result: P2Y11 is in nanometer proximity to CaV1.2 and PKA at the sarcolemma of arterial myocytes. GSD super-resolution microscopy revealed that P2Y11, CaV1.2, and PKAcat form clusters at the sarcolemma with closest centroid distances of 59 nm (P2Y11-CaV1.2) and 58 nm (P2Y11-PKAcat) in human cells. Similar results were observed in mouse cells. Proximity ligation assay (PLA) detected robust fluorescent puncta for P2Y11-CaV1.2 and P2Y11-PKAcat pairs in both human and mouse cells, indicating proximity ≤40 nm. The percentage of overlap was significantly higher than simulated random distributions.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C57 provide strong evidence for nanoscale spatial organization using two independent high-resolution techniques (GSD microscopy and PLA). The GSD analysis includes appropriate quantification (cluster size, density, distance histograms) and statistical comparison to randomized distributions (C52). PLA experiments include proper negative controls (omission of primary antibodies). The convergence of two orthogonal methods strengthens the conclusion of nanometer proximity.

results.result: P2Y11 agonist NF546 and elevated glucose stimulate cAMP production in arterial myocytes, and this is blocked by P2Y11 inhibitor NF340. FRET-based cAMP imaging showed that NF546 (500 nM) and elevated glucose (15 mM in human, 20 mM in mouse) both induced cAMP synthesis. The NF546 response was prevented by P2Y11 inhibitor NF340 but not by P2Y1 or P2Y6 inhibitors. Simultaneous application of glucose + NF546 produced similar cAMP levels as either stimulus alone, suggesting a common pathway. NF340 blocked both NF546 and glucose effects, while forskolin (bypassing P2Y11) still stimulated cAMP. Human cells showed significantly larger cAMP responses than mouse cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C69 demonstrate P2Y11-mediated cAMP signaling using FRET biosensors with appropriate pharmacological controls. The selectivity of NF340 for P2Y11 is validated by testing other P2Y inhibitors (C59). The non-additive effect of glucose + NF546 (C65) supports a common pathway. Osmotic controls with mannitol (C64) rule out osmotic effects. The forskolin control (C67) confirms that the cAMP machinery is intact after NF340 treatment. The species difference (C69) is noted but not fully explained.

results.result: P2Y11 inhibitor NF340 prevents glucose-induced increases in LTCC activity, Ser1928 phosphorylation, and vasoconstriction. In human and mouse arterial myocytes, NF340 blocked glucose-induced enhancement of LTCC currents (IBa) and Ser1928 phosphorylation. In pressurized mouse cerebral arteries, NF340 prevented glucose-induced vasoconstriction. The P2Y6 inhibitor MRS2578 did not prevent glucose effects on LTCC activity or Ser1928 phosphorylation, though it reduced basal arterial tone (consistent with P2Y6's role in myogenic tone). The P2Y1 inhibitor MRS2179 also did not affect glucose-induced vasoconstriction.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C82 demonstrate that P2Y11 is necessary for glucose effects using the selective inhibitor NF340 across multiple readouts (electrophysiology, Western blots, arterial diameter). The specificity is strengthened by showing that P2Y6 and P2Y1 inhibitors do not prevent glucose effects (C73, C77, C79, C82), though P2Y6 inhibition affects basal tone as expected from prior literature (C80). The K+ response control (C81) confirms that arteries remain responsive after inhibitor treatment.

results.result: P2Y11 agonist NF546 recapitulates glucose effects on LTCC activity, Ser1928 phosphorylation, and vasoconstriction in a PKA-dependent manner. NF546 increased LTCC currents in human and mouse arterial myocytes with similar magnitude to glucose. The non-hydrolyzable ATP analog ATPγS (a P2Y11 agonist) also enhanced LTCC activity. NF546 elevated Ser1928 phosphorylation in arterial lysates. PKA inhibitors (PKI, rpcAMP) prevented NF546-induced LTCC potentiation. NF546 caused vasoconstriction in pressurized arteries but did not induce further constriction in arteries already exposed to glucose. Arteries from S1928A knockin mice (lacking the PKA phosphorylation site) failed to constrict to NF546.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C93 demonstrate that P2Y11 activation is sufficient to mimic glucose effects. The use of multiple P2Y11 agonists (NF546, ATPγS) strengthens the conclusion (C83-C86). PKA inhibitor experiments (C88) establish PKA dependence. The lack of additivity between glucose and NF546 (C90-C91) supports a common pathway. The S1928A mouse experiments (C92) provide genetic validation that Ser1928 phosphorylation is required for NF546 effects. Appropriate controls (K+ response in S1928A mice, C93) are included.

results.result: P2Y11 inhibitor NF340 prevents chronic glucose-induced increases in LTCC activity and Ser1928 phosphorylation. In an organ culture model (48 hr incubation), arteries exposed to 20 mM glucose showed enhanced LTCC open probability (nPo) and elevated Ser1928 phosphorylation compared to 10 mM glucose controls. These effects were not observed with 20 mM mannitol (osmotic control) and were completely prevented by co-incubation with NF340. In S1928A mice, LTCC activity was similar at 10 mM and 20 mM glucose, confirming the requirement for Ser1928 phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C99 extend the acute findings to chronic hyperglycemia using single-channel recordings and an organ culture model. The mannitol control (C95) rules out osmotic effects. NF340 prevention (C96, C98) demonstrates P2Y11 involvement in chronic glucose effects. The S1928A mouse data (C99) provides genetic confirmation. The 48-hour timeframe is physiologically relevant for modeling diabetic conditions.

results.result: Background and rationale for investigating P2Y11 in glucose-induced vascular dysfunction. Prior work established that elevated glucose increases vascular reactivity through PKA-mediated LTCC potentiation via Ser1928 phosphorylation. Glucose triggers autocrine nucleotide release, which can activate P2Y receptors. P2Y11 is the only Gs-coupled P2Y receptor and could activate PKA via adenylyl cyclase. While P2Y11 has been identified in humans and other species, its presence in mice is uncertain (gene not found at expected genomic location), though pharmacological and annotation data suggest a P2Y11-like receptor may exist in rodents.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C28 provide the scientific rationale and are primarily based on established literature (citations provided). The authors accurately represent prior knowledge about glucose effects on vascular function (C11-C17), nucleotide release (C18-C21), P2Y receptor diversity (C22-C24), and the uncertain status of P2Y11 in mice (C27-C28). These background claims appropriately set up the research question.

results.result: Discussion and interpretation: P2Y11/AC/PKA/CaV1.2 nanodomain model for glucose signaling compartmentalization. The authors propose that P2Y11, AC, PKA, and CaV1.2 form a nanomolecular complex that enables PKA-mediated LTCC potentiation without affecting K+ channels (which would cause vasodilation). This spatial organization may be facilitated by AKAP150/79 scaffold proteins. Glucose metabolism generates ATP, which is released through various transporters and activates P2Y11 in this nanodomain. This model explains how glucose-induced PKA activation leads to vasoconstriction rather than the traditional vasodilation associated with PKA.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C116 present a mechanistic model integrating the experimental findings. While the proximity data (C7-C8, C47-C57) support spatial organization, several aspects remain speculative: the specific AC isoform involved (C104), the complete composition of the nanodomain (C105), the role of AKAP proteins (C107-C111), and the identity of ATP transporters (C113-C114). The authors appropriately qualify these as speculations and acknowledge that confirmation is beyond the scope of the study (C105). The model is plausible and consistent with the data but requires additional experimental validation.

results.result: Additional background on P2Y11 receptor properties and cardiovascular relevance. P2Y11 stimulates adenylyl cyclase to produce cAMP and has been associated with positive inotropic effects in cardiomyocytes. A P2Y11 polymorphism is linked to increased cardiovascular risk. ATP activates P2Y11 with EC50 of 1.8-17 μM, and the receptor shows selectivity for ATP-derived nucleotides (ATPγS > dATP > ATP >>> ADP) with minimal response to UTP/UDP.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C123 accurately summarize established knowledge about P2Y11 pharmacology and cardiovascular function, supported by appropriate citations. This background information contextualizes the current findings within the broader P2Y11 literature.
